title: Get Ready To Explore An Artist And Organisation
objective: Choose useful questions about an artist and an arts organisation, ready for a live or active experience.

blocks.text: BUILD · Art · Trinity Arts Award Explore. Get Ready To Explore An Artist And Organisation.
Objective: Choose useful questions about an artist and an arts organisation, ready for a live or active experience.
Success evidence: Own questions for both roles, a rehearsed way to take part, a preparation label and an exact location for this work.
You can explore through looking, listening, asking and trying. Choose a way to take part that works for you. You do not need to share private facts about your life.
We may go to them, they may come in, or we may meet live on screen. The route comes from the current slot card. No meeting is promised by this deck.
40-minute lesson frame. Staff may extend or split the real experience across sessions.

This deck serves Explore Part B, Explore. Part B requires at least one artist AND at least one arts organisation, through live or active experience. Desk research alone fails; archives and prerecorded video are preparation only. Explore has four parts, each a distinct activity. Overall Pass allows ONE Attempted. Any Not Attempted = Below Pass. The whole Explore portfolio has a 10-file cap, organised digitally by part. The three assessment areas are art form knowledge and understanding, creativity, and communication. Results are Pass or Below Pass only. Only an adviser trained at Explore may assess; delivery is through a validated centre. Neither local training nor validation is asserted as confirmed here. Advisers must not write plans, reviews or evidence for pupils. Scribe or record the pupil's own words and check them back unchanged. Core, Extend and Challenge are support routes within Explore and retain the live or active requirement. An evidence locator names the filename plus page, slide or timecode. Read the current PRACTITIONER_SLOT and ORG_SLOT from tools/artsaward/SLOTS.json; no candidate name or date is embedded here. R1 pupils visit, R2 the artist or arts organisation comes in, R3 live remote exchange: all remain unconfirmed until actually arranged. Do not treat a recorded video as a live exchange. Source: tools/artsaward/SPEC.json, Explore and universal rules. Today is preparation; it cannot complete Part B. Teach the roles with the visible classroom model and question cards. The adult is demonstrating, not impersonating a named artist or claiming to represent the eventual organisation. Confirm the actual artist and organisation through the shared slots before treating later activities as the experience. A single genuine experience may serve both elements if each is separately identified and evidenced. Record unmet arrangements as next actions. Use the stage guidance for concrete support; lesson timing does not force a real exchange into forty minutes.

stages.title: Arrival · retrieve
stages.data-ta1: Offer actual pupil work to retrieve. Accept a point or gesture and read the chosen detail back without supplying a personal meaning.

blocks.text: From making to finding out
Bring a drawing or paper piece from your recent work. Find a choice you made in it.
You might point to a line, a fold, a join or a shape. What did your hand do to make that part?
Now think about someone else who makes art. What would you like to find out about how they work?
An artist makes art. An arts organisation is a group that helps art happen. We will call it the arts group on these pages.
It may help people make, show or learn about art. Its work is more than the name on a door.
Part B needs a real way to explore both. Today we get ready.

stages.title: Starter · create the need
stages.data-ta1: Make the simple paper shape in front of pupils. Use the turn to distinguish a making choice from a display choice; claim no outside experience.

blocks.text: The work and the way to see it
Look at a paper shape the adult has made. First it faces the wall. Then the adult turns it so the class can see.
The folds belong to the making. The space and the way it is shown affect how people can see it.
Which would you ask the maker about? Which might you ask the group that shows the work?
These roles can link. A person may make art and also help run a group. We still need to find out about both jobs.
This classroom model helps us form questions. It is not a record of the Part B experience.

stages.title: I Do · model
stages.data-ta1: Label this as a rehearsal model. Show an actual fold and only answer from this classroom action. Do not invent an artist biography or organisation reply.

blocks.text: Rehearsal model: a question from a detail
Watch the adult turn a detail into a question. They point to a fold that makes the paper stand.
They first ask, 'Is it good?' That could bring a yes or no, but it tells us little about the work.
They try, 'How did you make that part stand?' Now the question points to a clear part and asks about a choice.
The adult can show that fold on their own paper. Watch the action as well as the words.
For the arts group, a different question might be, 'How do you help people see work like this?'
That asks about the group's work, not the maker's fold. Both questions have a job.
A useful question can start with how, what or why. It should help you find out something you do not know yet.
You may ask through speech, a written card, a picture or an adult who reads your words. Keep the question yours.
After a reply, you could point to the detail again or ask for a step to be shown. Practise that here; the real reply comes later.

blocks.title: A detail can lead to a question
blocks.caption: Look, notice, ask, then follow up.
blocks.alt: Four boxes link looking at a detail, noticing a choice, asking a question and following up.

stages.title: We Do · everyone commits
stages.data-ta1: Suggested matches: A/C artist, B/D arts group. Accept a reasoned overlap where a maker also works for the organisation. All card text is supplied below.

data.heading: Choose a question with a purpose
data.instruction: Everyone commits to a question before we compare. These classroom examples help us rehearse; they are not replies from the real artist or arts group.

items.label: You want to know how the artist made a thin curved mark. Which question points to that detail?
items.feedback: This question points to a mark in the work. The artist can explain the tool or action they used.

options.label: What tool made this thin curve?

items.label: You want to know how an arts group helps people take part. Which question fits?
items.feedback: This asks about a role the group may have. Find out what the real group actually does.

options.label: How do you help someone try a new art tool?
Did you make every picture in the world?

items.label: No live or active session is confirmed yet. What should your preparation card say?
items.feedback: A preparation card helps you get ready. It does not prove that a real session took place.

options.label: The real experience is still to be arranged.

data.discussion: Now make your own question for the artist and one for the arts group. You may point, sign or ask through an adult. Keep both real experience needs open.
data.staffNote: These are illustrative questions, not a booked programme or substitute for Explore Part B. Keep artist exploration and arts organisation exploration distinct.

stages.title: I Do 2 · connect
stages.data-ta1: Read the current PRACTITIONER_SLOT and ORG_SLOT with the pupil. Keep an empty or unconfirmed slot explicit. No completed-experience check is awarded for rehearsal.

blocks.text: Preparation is a step, not the whole job
A page, photo or video can help you think of a question. It cannot answer every question about what a person or group does.
A printed answer does not let you ask for a closer view. A recorded film cannot respond to your own try.
In a live or active experience, you can take part in what is really offered. You might ask a question, try a process, explore a display with a guide or respond to a live demonstration.
The exact activity depends on the real artist and arts group. Staff will check what is arranged and what you can use.
If the slot cards are blank, keep your questions. Leave names and dates open. Do not turn a guess into a fact.
Your preparation is useful. It gets you ready to explore both the artist and the group when the experience is arranged.

boxes.head: PREPARE
boxes.line1: read, watch and form a question

boxes.head: EXPLORE
boxes.line1: take part in the real experience

blocks.title: Preparation leads into real exploration
blocks.caption: Keep preparation and real experience clearly labelled.
blocks.alt: Two panels distinguish reading and question preparation from taking part in the real live or active experience.

stages.title: We Do 2 · lab
stages.data-ta1: Act as a rehearsal partner only. For the group question, check clarity rather than supplying a fictional response.

blocks.text: Test a question, not a made-up answer
Choose a question about the adult's classroom paper shape. Ask it in the way you prefer.
The adult will answer from the shape they made. Point to the part their answer helped you notice.
Now test a question for the arts group. Ask a partner or adult to say what they think the question means. They do not need to pretend to run that group.
If the question is not clear, change a word or add a sketch. Try it once more.
Label this work rehearsal. Keep the question you want to use later. Do not copy the classroom answer into the place for the real artist's reply.

stages.title: Independent · evidence
stages.data-ta1: All tiers keep a question for both elements and the later live/active requirement. Scribe verbatim, or support a pupil-selected picture/gesture with an accurate note.

blocks.text: Make your preparation card
Choose what you want to find out about the artist and the arts group. Keep both on your sheet.
Link each question to something you noticed. A word, arrow or quick sketch can show that link.
Check the current slot cards with staff. If they name a confirmed activity, note how you could take part. If not, mark that part to be arranged.
Plan how to keep your own response after the real experience. You might use a sample, a short note or an agreed recording.
Save today's card in Part B and label it preparation. Name the filename and page, slide or timecode so you can find it again.

items: Core · use the sheet prompts to choose a question for the artist and one for the arts group. Point, speak or write your choices. Practise how to ask and label the work preparation. Both still need real live or active exploration.
Extend · make the same two-part preparation in your own layout. Link each question to something you noticed. Plan what you might ask or try in the real experience and how to keep the record.
Challenge · keep both real experience needs. Test a follow-up question that could help you find out more. Say when you would use it. Do not invent an answer before the experience.

stages.title: Exit · Audience and Influence
stages.data-ta1: Record access requests and the next arrangement. Check both preparation questions are findable without marking Part B complete.

blocks.text: Keep a clear next step
Show someone where your artist question and arts group question sit. Ask them to find the preparation label.
Say what you hope to ask, see or try when the real experience is ready. You may point to your planned action.
Tell staff if you need a closer view, a quiet space, a different grip or help reading your words.
Keep the card ready for the next lesson. There is still a real artist and a real arts group to explore.
A good question opens that door. It does not claim you have already gone through it.
